White is actually winning on the board here, so king safety is not the most relevant diagnosis. The important issue is that the belief state has problems to fix around this CSP reseed/collapse moment.

This is the key collapse diagnosis. Just before collapse, belief surprisingly tracked all 3 remaining black pawns correctly in the top world, but it failed to model black's remaining non-pawn piece, the king, on e6. When the black king captured the white knight on f5, white could not see the capturer identity and no top world connected it to the king, so reseeding scrambled pawns that were previously correct. This points toward individual piece/pawn probability tracking through the board and smarter reseeding that preserves high-confidence pawns while moving the likely capturer, under strict rules like bishop color and pawn direction plus softer priors.
White genuinely did not know whether the black pawn was defended. A safer plan was to push the h-pawn once the path was cleared instead of trying to capture with the king.
Black is already so much material down that the exact move likely does not change the result. Trading a pawn for the opponent's queen may be the best practical thing black can do in that position.

White could capture on d4 with either the knight or queen and chose the more valuable piece. In fog, that is probably wrong: prefer taking with the least valuable piece first when the target square may be further defended or attacked by the opponent.
